questions.stem: A 58-year-old man presented with a 4-day history of low-grade fever, cough, and wheezing. He was known to have COPD. His chest X-ray showed no infiltrates. He was sent home with prescriptions for azithromycin and prednisone for treatment of presumed COPD exacerbation. Two days later, his blood cultures returned positive.
questions.lead_in: What organism should prompt urgent re-evaluation?
questions.explanation: Staphylococcus aureus S. aureus is an aggressive pathogen that can cause a variety of potentially life-threatening syndromes. When recovered Induration of ≥5 mm Induration of ≥10 mm Induration of ≥15 mm HIV infected persons Recent immigrants (less than 5 years) from high-prevalence countries Considered positive in any person Recent contact of a person with TB Injection drug users Persons with fibrotic changes on chest radiograph consistent with prior TB Residents and employees of high-risk congregate settings Patients with organ transplants Mycobacteriology laboratory personnel Persons who are immunosuppressed for other reasons Children less than 4 years Persons with clinical conditions that place them at high risk Infants, children, and adolescents exposed to adults in high-risk categories from blood cultures, it should not be regarded as a contaminant. Patients with blood cultures that are positive for S. aureus require thorough evaluation for sites of infection, exclusion of infective endocarditis, and parenteral IV antibiotic therapy.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q14

questions.stem: A 46-year-old man presented with a 5-day history of dyspnea and a nonproductive cough. Four weeks earlier he had returned from a holiday in West Africa where he had bought components for drums, which he then crafted himself. He had a history of hypertension, obesity, and type 2 diabetes. On examination, he appeared ill. His blood pressure was 85/46mmHg, heart rate was 115 beats/minute, respiratory rate was 32 breaths/minute, and oxygen saturations were 86% on 4LPM oxygen. He required urgent intubation and transfer to the critical care unit. Investigations: CXR: small bilateral effusions seen with cardiomegaly 4 sets of blood cultures positive at 12 hours with grampositive rods
questions.lead_in: What infection prevention intervention is most appropriate?

options.text: Doxycycline prophylaxis for healthcare workers exposed to droplets
Immunization for all healthcare worker providing direct care

questions.explanation: Standard precautions only These materials used as drum heads can be contaminated with anthrax spores. The patient is not at risk to those around him and therefore requires only standard precautions. The exposure does need to be pursued, and there may be family and friends that require chemoprophylaxis. The healthcare workers that came into contact with him do not need immunization or chemoprophylaxis.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q42

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man in Kyrgyzstan presented with painless lesions on both arms. The lesions had begun as pruritic papules but had then enlarged, becoming vesicular, coalescing into bullae and developing significant local and spreading edema. He had systemic symptoms of chills and fever. The patient worked on a farm and had handled cattle 6 days earlier. On examination there was extensive edema and hemorrhagic bullae in both arms. He had tender lymphadenopathy in both axillae. His temperature was 37.9°C. Swabs were taken of the vesicular fluid, and a full-thickness punch biopsy was taken. Blood cultures were also sent. Microscopy using polychrome methylene blue stain showed blue-colored bacilli with light pink-colored capsules.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate antimicrobial?
questions.explanation: Benzylpenicillin Penicillin is the drug of choice in naturally occurring anthrax. This can either be oral or intramuscular in mild uncomplicated cutaneous anthrax or intravenous in complicated or severe cutaneous anthrax. Penicillin is used in combination with other antimicrobials such as clindamycin and ciprofloxacin in inhalational anthrax or with streptomycin in gastrointestinal infection. (Image from Assessments. In Cohen J, Powderly W , Opal S, eds. Infectious Diseases. 4th ed. Elsevier; 2017.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q41

questions.stem: There was a reported bioterrorist release of anthrax spores in a crowd at a professional football game in an outdoor stadium. The announcement about the release of the spores was made 3 hours after the game ended. Rapid testing confirmed contamination at the stadium with anthrax spores, and PCR confirmed Bacillus anthracis.
questions.lead_in: What would be the most appropriate immediate management of those who attended the game?

options.text: Anthrax immune globulin and 3 doses of anthrax vaccine
Hospitalization with respiratory isolation for those in contaminated seats
Self-taken nasal swab to determine whether exposed

questions.explanation: Prophylaxis with ciprofloxacin or doxycycline Nasal swabs are not indicated in this setting as everyone at the stadium would be presumed to have been exposed. Although ciprofloxacin and doxycycline are contraindicated in pregnancy and in children, they are both recommended as prophylaxis for anthrax exposure. If sensitivities of B. anthracis return as penicillin-susceptible, the regimen can then be changed to amoxicillin. Hospitalization is not required unless symptomatic. Anthrax immune globulin is indicated for the treatment of inhalational anthrax. Anthrax vaccine may be indicated for exposure in a mass-incident exposure such as this, but not in combination with immune globulin.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 9 Q26

questions.question: A woman travels to Tanzania and climbs Mount Kilimanjaro. She presents with fever and an eschar. List 3 organisms on the differential.
questions.question_raw: A woman travels to Tanzania and climbs Mount Kilimanjaro. She presents with a fever and eschar.
questions.model_answer: (1) Rickettsia africae (African tick-bite fever) - the leading cause of fever with eschar in sub-Saharan Africa travelers; produces multiple inoculation eschars. (2) Francisella tularensis (ulceroglandular tularaemia) - eschar/ulcer with regional lymphadenopathy. (3) Bacillus anthracis (cutaneous anthrax) - painless black eschar. (Scrub typhus, Orientia tsutsugamushi, is an alternative but is not endemic to this region.)
questions.beyond_mandell: Only R. africae is grounded in this chapter (Table 185.3, sub-Saharan Africa, 100% multiple eschars); tularaemia and anthrax as eschar causes are from standard travel/ID sources (IDSA, CDC Yellow Book), not this chapter.

cohort_answer.text: African trypanosomiasis; Tularemia; Rickettsia africae (African tick bite fever); Scrub typhus; Bacillus anthracis; Plague.

questions.question: A peripheral hospital transports a specimen from a patient with hemorrhagic bullous lesions to your laboratory. The isolate is non-motile and non-hemolytic, and Gram stain shows large gram-positive bacilli.
questions.question_raw: There is a patient with "hemorrhagic bullous lesions" in a peripheral hospital. It has been transported to your laboratory: non-motile, non-hemolytic. Gram stain shows large GPB.

parts.text: What two things should you do right away?
What three tests would you use to identify the organism?
You wish to send this specimen to the reference laboratory. What are three issues you need to address when transporting specimens?

parts_raw.text: What 2 things should you do right away?
What 3 tests would you use to identify the organism?
You wish to send this specimen off to the reference laboratory. What are 3 issues you need to do when transporting specimens?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Notify the laboratory/supervisor and infection control that anthrax is suspected, and stop routine bench manipulation — handle the isolate only in a biosafety cabinet under BSL-2 (or higher) conditions, since B. anthracis sporulates on agar and can cause laboratory-acquired infection. (2) Notify the local public health department immediately and refer the isolate to a Laboratory Response Network reference (level B/C) laboratory for confirmation. b) (1) Demonstration of lysis by gamma phage; (2) detection of the capsule by direct fluorescent antibody; (3) identification of toxin genes (PA/LF/EF) by PCR assay — all typically performed at a reference laboratory. c) (1) Package per ASM/IATA rules for a Category A infectious substance (triple-layer packaging, appropriate labelling); (2) transport at the correct temperature for the specimen type (e.g., swabs/culture at 2°C–8°C, swabs for PCR frozen at −70°C without transport medium); (3) notify the receiving reference laboratory in advance that anthrax is suspected.

questions.question: Name 1 rickettsial, 1 bacterial (non-rickettsial) and 1 viral cause of eschar and the clinical syndrome that each causes.

parts.text: Name 1 rickettsial, 1 bacterial (non-rickettsial) and 1 viral cause of eschar and the clinical syndrome that it causes.

parts_raw.text: Name 1 rickettsial, 1 bacterial (non-rickettsia) and 1 viral cause of eschar and the clinical syndrome that it causes.

questions.model_answer: (1) Rickettsial: Rickettsia africae - African tick-bite fever (fever, multiple inoculation eschars, regional lymphadenopathy). (2) Bacterial (non-rickettsial): Francisella tularensis - ulceroglandular tularaemia (cutaneous ulcer/eschar with tender regional lymphadenopathy). (3) Viral: Variola/orthopoxvirus (smallpox or, historically, vaccinia) - vesiculopustular lesions that crust into eschars.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the rickettsial cause is in this chapter (Table 185.3). Bacterial (tularaemia) and viral (orthopoxvirus) eschar causes are from standard ID sources, not this chapter.

questions.question: A blood culture is positive for Bacillus.
questions.question_raw: Blood culture is positive for Bacillus.

parts.text: How do you tell if it is B. anthracis, and what are the results of the tests?
What is another major Bacillus species implicated in human disease?

parts_raw.text: How to tell if anthracis and results from tests?
What is another major bacillus species implicated in human disease?

questions.model_answer: a) B. anthracis is a large gram-positive bacillus with rapid, non-hemolytic growth on blood agar, is non-motile and catalase-positive, and forms a prominent poly-d-γ-glutamic acid capsule in CO2/bicarbonate — features that distinguish it from most other Bacillus spp. (which are motile and beta-hemolytic). Colonies show a "Medusa's head/comet tail" margin and a tenacious "whipped egg white" texture. Definitive confirmation: lysis by gamma phage (positive), capsule detected by direct fluorescent antibody (positive), and toxin genes identified by PCR (positive); it is typically penicillin-susceptible. b) Bacillus cereus.

cohort_answer.text: B. anthracis: (non)Motility, (non)hemolysis, Gamma phage testing or PCR, and pen S. Non motile, spore forming, non hemolysis. Other bacillus involved in human diseases: B. cereus: gastroenteritis, bacteremia. B. subtilis = rare cause of pneumonia, bacteremia, septicemia (usually in patients with hematologic malignancy or some other severe immune compromise) and may cause foodborne disease (diarrheal illness similar to B. cereus). B. licheniformis = associated with outbreak of bacteremia in immunocompromised due to contaminated cotton wool, and a well-established cause of central-line infections. All other species are motiles or +/- motil. R to pen except B. cereus biovar anthracis.

questions.question: Bacillus anthracis.

parts.text: What laboratory test do you do to distinguish it from non-anthracis strains?

parts_raw.text: A) What lab test do you do to distinguish it from non-anthracis strains?

questions.model_answer: a) Definitive confirmation of B. anthracis requires demonstration of lysis by gamma phage, detection of the capsule by direct fluorescent antibody, and identification of toxin genes by PCR assay (generally performed at a reference laboratory). Supporting bench features that separate it from other Bacillus spp. are non-motility, non-hemolysis, and catalase positivity.

cohort_answer.text: Lysis of gamma-phage; Detection of PGA capsule by fluorescent antibody; Identify toxin genes by PCR; MALDI-TOF. [Background: B. anthracis is nonhemolytic on sheep/horse blood agar and nonmotile, whereas most other clinical isolates are motile and beta-hemolytic]

questions.question: Bacillus anthracis.

parts.text: What does the Gram stain look like?

parts_raw.text: B) What does the gram stain look like?

questions.model_answer: a) Large (1–1.5 µm × 3–8 µm) gram-positive bacilli. In culture they form long chains with prominent central or paracentral oval spores that do not stain (appearing as clear areas within the bacilli) and do not cause swelling of the rod. In the presence of CO2/bicarbonate the organism is encapsulated. In infected tissue, bacteria occur singly or in short chains of two to three bacilli without spores.

cohort_answer.text: Large encapsulated gram positive bacilli; Long chains with central oval spores (clearing); Aerobic; Non-hemolytic; Spore-forming; Colonies look like "Medusa's head" aka "comet tail" referring to slightly curled periphery

questions.question: A government official opens an envelope and white powder is released. The letter says it contains anthrax spores.
questions.question_raw:
Q27 (2003 PM)
Government official opens envelope, white powder released. Letter says it is anthrax spores.

parts.text: What three immediate public health measures would you take?

parts_raw.text: What 3 immediate public health measures would you take?

questions.model_answer:
(1) Immediately notify public health, law enforcement/police and the hospital emergency preparedness team; isolate and secure the room (stop air handling, close doors, do not further disturb the powder) and have the envelope handled and transported as evidence to a designated reference laboratory, with the laboratory alerted that anthrax is suspected so staff can work under BSL-3 containment.
(2) Identify and register everyone potentially exposed in the room/mail path; have them remove contaminated clothing into sealed bags and wash exposed skin with soap and water (no bleach on skin); person-to-person transmission does not occur, so routine practices only and no quarantine.
(3) Start post-exposure prophylaxis for exposed persons — ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO BID (or doxycycline 100 mg PO BID) for 60 days plus anthrax vaccine where available — pending environmental testing, and discontinue if the powder tests negative for Bacillus anthracis; provide risk communication to the exposed and to the public.
questions.beyond_mandell: CDC/PHAC anthrax bioterrorism response and PEP recommendations.

cohort_answer.text: Contact Public Health; Notify lab on suspicion of anthrax to confirm dx; Contact tracing; Post-exposure ppx; Decontaminate all contacts thoroughly

questions.question: A government official opens an envelope and white powder is released; the letter states it contains anthrax spores.
questions.question_raw:
Q27 (2003 PM)
Government official opens envelope, white powder released. Letter says it is anthrax spores.

parts.text: What prophylaxis would you recommend to a patient exposed to anthrax spores?

parts_raw.text: B) What ppx would you recommend to a patient exposed to anthrax spores?

questions.model_answer: a) Antibiotic postexposure prophylaxis for 60 days plus postexposure anthrax immunization. First-line antibiotic: ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO BID or doxycycline 100 mg PO BID (equal preferred agents); alternatives levofloxacin 750 mg daily, moxifloxacin 400 mg daily, or clindamycin 600 mg q8h. For penicillin-susceptible strains: amoxicillin 1 g q8h or penicillin VK 500 mg q6h. Anthrax vaccine adsorbed (AVA) is given as 3 subcutaneous doses at weeks 0, 2, and 4; the antibiotic regimen is adjusted once the isolate's susceptibility profile is known.

cohort_answer.text: Cipro 500mg PO BID or Doxy 100mg PO BID x 60 days. Alternatives: Levofloxacin, Moxifloxacin, Clindamycin. If PCN susceptible: Amox 1g PO TID or Pen VK 500mg PO q6h. Vaccine 3 doses at 0, 2, 4 weeks

questions.question: A government official opens an envelope and white powder is released; the letter states it contains anthrax spores.
questions.question_raw:
Q27 (2003 PM)
Government official opens envelope, white powder released. Letter says it is anthrax spores.

parts.text: Name three sites of infection and the mechanism by which those infections occur.

parts_raw.text: C) 3 sites of infection and mechanism of how those infections occur

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Cutaneous anthrax — introduction of spores into the skin, usually through trivial trauma, from contact with contaminated animal products (wool, hair, hides, bone, meat) or injection of contaminated heroin. (2) Inhalational (pulmonary) anthrax — inhalation of spore-laden dust; particles smaller than 5 µm reach the alveoli, are carried to mediastinal lymph nodes where they germinate, producing a mediastinal (not primary airspace) process. (3) Gastrointestinal anthrax — ingestion of spores/vegetative forms in undercooked or uncooked contaminated meat, causing oropharyngeal or intestinal disease.

cohort_answer.text: Cutaneous anthrax – contact with contaminated animal source with trivial skin trauma (wool, hair, bone, meat, horns, hides), or injection of heroin contaminated with spores. Inhalational anthrax – inhalation of spores. Gastrointestinal anthrax – ingesting undercooked meat from infected animal

questions.question: A farmer on prednisone who cleans barns develops necrotizing pneumonia; Gram stain of blood shows gram-positive bacilli.
questions.question_raw: Q4 (2003 PM). Necrotizing pneumonia. Farmer on prednisone, cleans barns; develops necrotizing pneumonia. Gram stain of blood shows GPB.

parts.text: State the diagnosis and its clinical, microbiologic, and epidemiologic features.

questions.model_answer: a) Diagnosis: Rhodococcus equi infection. Clinical: opportunistic pathogen affecting immunocompromised hosts (corticosteroids, HIV); most commonly causes subacute cavitary/necrotizing pneumonia that can mimic tuberculosis, often with bacteremia. Microbiologic: pleomorphic gram-positive coccobacilli, partially/weakly acid-fast; slow-growing colonies that are initially small and diphtheroid-like, becoming mucoid salmon-pink over 4–7 days; catalase-positive; can be mistaken for a diphtheroid contaminant or mycobacterium. Epidemiologic: found in soil worldwide and associated with grazing animals, especially horses/foals and swine; farm and manure/barn exposure is the classic risk, with acquisition by inhalation, wound inoculation, or ingestion. Treatment uses combinations of intracellularly active agents (e.g., macrolide plus rifampin, with a fluoroquinolone, vancomycin, or carbapenem) for a prolonged course in the immunocompromised.
questions.beyond_mandell: Not covered in the B. anthracis chapter; answer drawn from Mandell's Rhodococcus/coryneform bacteria chapter and standard ID knowledge.

cohort_answer.text: Rhodococcus equi. Clinical: mainly affects immunocompromised hosts (recognized opportunistic infection in HIV); pulmonary infections most common (cavitary lesions, lung consolidation, indistinguishable from TB). Micro: pleomorphic GPR (coccoid to bacillary), early colonies small/white (resembling diphtheroids, contaminant risk), salmon-pink colonies appear days 4-7, sometimes stains acid fast (confused with mycobacteria). Epi: found in soil worldwide, thrives in marine/freshwater habitats, infects land/water animals; human acquisition via inhalation, wound/mucous membrane inoculation, or ingestion from exposure to domesticated animals (horses, pigs). Treatment: coryneform bacteria uniformly susceptible to glycopeptides (vancomycin, teicoplanin), most susceptible to daptomycin/linezolid; R. equi usually susceptible to vancomycin, teicoplanin, erythromycin, FQ, rifampin, carbapenems, aminoglycosides, linezolid; macrolide + rifampin combination most commonly used for minimum 2 months in immunocompromised host.

questions.question: List 1 infection (causative organism not required) under each category that causes an eschar.

parts_raw.text: List 1 infection (causative organism not required) under each category that cause an eschar - Rickettsial

questions.model_answer: a) Rickettsial: African tick-bite fever (Rickettsia africae) - alternatives include scrub typhus, Mediterranean spotted fever, rickettsialpox. b) Bacterial (non-rickettsial): Ulceroglandular tularaemia (Francisella tularensis); alternatively cutaneous anthrax or plague. c) Virus: Orthopoxvirus infection - smallpox/vaccinia (crusting eschar).
questions.beyond_mandell: Only part a) is grounded in this chapter (Table 185.3 lists rickettsioses with eschar). Bacterial and viral eschar causes are from standard ID sources, not this chapter.

cohort_answer.text: Rickettsial: Scrub typhus, murine typhus, epidemic typhus, african tick bite fever (Orientia tsutsugamushi, rickettsia africae). Bacterial (non-rickettsial): Tularemia, plague (Francisella tularensis, yersinia pestis); Ecthyma (pseudomonas). Virus: Smallpox, vaccinia
